claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Internal boundaries in the lamellar colonies serve as microcrack-initiation sites during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Hot deformation followed by uniform aging can refine lamellar spacing.
Hot deformation followed by uniform aging can improve phase-boundary integrity.
Overheating or excessive thermal exposure can cause excessive grain growth or over-aging.
Processing can preserve the lamellar-colony structure while refining it.
Reduced lamellar spacing minimizes stress concentrations.
Enhanced boundary bonding suppresses the development of microcracks.
Decreasing lamella width and enhancing interfacial cohesion reduce defect density at internal boundaries.
Reduced boundary-defect density and enhanced interfacial cohesion mitigate microcrack initiation and propagation.
Lamellar refinement increases load-bearing capacity and tensile strength.
Suppression of microcracking increases the capacity for plastic deformation and tensile ductility.
The tailored thermo-mechanically processed material will have higher room-temperature tensile strength than the unmodified alloy.
The tailored thermo-mechanically processed material will have greater room-temperature elongation at failure than the unmodified alloy.
The conventional baseline has coarser lamellar colonies and numerous internal stress concentrators associated with room-temperature brittleness.
The proposed improvement is limited to eutectic high-entropy alloys possessing lamellar-colony structures.
Alloys lacking lamellar colonies or having fundamentally different morphologies might not benefit from the proposed processing.
The magnitude of the property enhancement depends on processing conditions.
